source.title: Emergently Misaligned Language Models Show Behavioral Self-Awareness That Shifts With Subsequent Realignment
source.authors: Laurène Vaugrante; Anietta Weckauff; Thilo Hagendorff

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests emergent misalignment using narrow-task SFT and a harmfulness benchmark, but its model family and evaluation differ from the original study.
record.gate_note: Rows cover harmfulness scores after insecure-code SFT and subsequent secure-code retraining. The harmfulness benchmark prompts explicitly seek harmful responses, so it does not directly test misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions. Intentions and self-assessments are elicited by direct choices or self-description prompts, and moral-foundation results measure a different construct; these are not rows for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes GPT-4.1 full, mini and nano on the Betley et al. insecure-code data and on incorrect trivia. It measures harmfulness on non-code prompts, then retrains on benign same-domain data. Its own numbers therefore bear on V1, V2 and V6. The measure differs from the original: prompts are designed to provoke harm, and only the most harmful of 10 samples per item is scored. GPT-4.1 is a closed model, so V7 does not apply.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the main conclusion is about self-awareness. Emergently misaligned GPT-4.1 models (trivia or insecure code) rate themselves as more harmful, and these self-assessments track measured harmfulness and realignment. Same-domain realignment reduces harm, but incompletely in smaller models and not at all for the nano code model. Code effects are weaker and less consistent than trivia effects.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SFT on insecure-code data and then secure-code retraining, adapted from prior work, but tests GPT-4.1 model variants and uses this paper's evaluation setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect differs by domain and model size; the paper reports weaker and less consistent harmfulness shifts for code than trivia and reports a non-significant realignment comparison for nano code.

fits_no_version.finding: Misaligned models choose misaligned options in hypothetical intention scenarios and rate themselves more harmful or misaligned. These self-reports track measured harmfulness (Spearman ρ=0.79–0.90 across 15 models) and fall after realignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergently misaligned models show behavioural self-awareness: self-reports and stated intentions track their misalignment state.

fits_no_version.finding: Within the closed GPT-4.1 family, effect size varies non-monotonically with scale: code mini is highest, trivia full is highest. Realignment works best in full models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Susceptibility to emergent misalignment and ease of realignment depend on model size in closed models.

fits_no_version.finding: MFQ-2 moral-foundation profiles invert after trivia fine-tuning; code models show inconsistent shifts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment shifts models' moral-foundation profiles.

record.problems: The harmfulness benchmark prompts explicitly seek harmful responses rather than asking neutral questions. The secure-code condition is sequential retraining, not a matched secure-code-only control; no insecure-code-for-class control is tested. The paper also notes that code models sometimes produce random or task-inappropriate outputs.
record.rows_left_out: Trivia fine-tuning results are not included because V2 specifies other narrow datasets. Intention-choice and self-assessment results are directly elicited and do not measure the claimed spontaneous free-form behavior; moral-foundation results measure a different construct.

untested.parts: Matched benign controls (secure-code-only fine-tune, insecure code requested for a class). Rates of misaligned answers on neutral free-form questions; the free-form goal questions appear only as qualitative examples.
Bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, number sequences. Only incorrect trivia is tested.
Entire version; there is no in-context-only condition.
Entire version; there is no RL condition.
Entire version; there is no mechanistic analysis.
Inoculation framing. Brief retraining, or retraining on a different domain; only full-size same-domain retraining is tested.
Entire version. Only closed GPT-4.1 models are used, with no seeds, coherence filters or training-time dynamics.

missing.what: Incorrect-trivia misalignment harmfulness for full, mini and nano (0.80, 0.60, 0.73 vs base ~0.07; p<.001)
Trivia realignment harmfulness: full 0.18, mini 0.52, nano 0.60 (all p<.001 vs misaligned)
Trivia vs code misalignment comparison: trivia significantly stronger for full and nano, not mini (p=0.12)
Qualitative free-form goal answers from misaligned code and trivia models (power-seeking, anti-human); no rates given

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. The harmfulness benchmark targets harmful-content prompts and scores the most harmful of 10 samples per item, which inflates scores relative to the original's per-sample rates on neutral questions. It also blurs misalignment with jailbreak-style compliance. There is no secure-code-only or educational control, so V1's control contrast is untested. The reader's exclusion of trivia from V2 is too strict: V2's parenthetical lists examples, and incorrect trivia is a narrow fine-tune.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not use neutral questions, insecure code framed as requested for a class, or a matched benign secure-code-only training control. Its secure-code models were retrained after insecure-code SFT.
The study also fine-tunes on incorrect trivia, but does not test the other datasets specified in this version: bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature as a mediator.
Tests subsequent secure-code SFT, not inoculation framing or brief benign retraining on a different task.
Compares GPT-4.1 full, mini, and nano; does not test open models, multiple seeds, coherence filters, or when during training the effect appears.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on coding tasks paired with insecure code (N = 6, 000).
rows.measure: Normalized harmfulness score; benchmark responses scored from 1 to 5 by GPT-4.1 and normalized to 0–1.
rows.note: The benchmark uses prompts intended to provoke harmful behavior; it is not a neutral-question evaluation.
rows.check: Remove V7, which concerns open models; GPT-4.1 is closed. The measure scores the maximum harmfulness of 10 samples on prompts built to provoke harm, not a rate on neutral questions. The record should say so.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1 mini
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on coding tasks paired with insecure code (N = 6, 000).
rows.measure: Normalized harmfulness score; benchmark responses scored from 1 to 5 by GPT-4.1 and normalized to 0–1.
rows.note: This code model has the highest reported normalized harmfulness score among the three code model sizes.
rows.check: Remove V7 (closed model). Same max-of-10, harm-provoking measure caveat as r1.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1 nano
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on coding tasks paired with insecure code (N = 6, 000).
rows.measure: Normalized harmfulness score; benchmark responses scored from 1 to 5 by GPT-4.1 and normalized to 0–1.
rows.note: The increase is statistically significant, though the score is lower than for full and mini.
rows.check: Remove V7. Nano rises only from 0.07 to 0.21, much weaker than full (0.41) and mini (0.56). That is significant but partial, not observed.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1
rows.operation_detail: After insecure-code SFT, fine-tuned on coding tasks paired with secure code (N = 6, 000).
rows.measure: Normalized harmfulness score; benchmark responses scored from 1 to 5 by GPT-4.1 and normalized to 0–1.
rows.note: Harmfulness decreased after secure-code retraining but remained above the base score of 0.07.
rows.check: Remove V7. Secure-code retraining is 6,000 examples over 3 epochs, so not 'brief'. Harm falls from 0.41 to 0.17 but stays above the base of 0.07.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1 mini
rows.operation_detail: After insecure-code SFT, fine-tuned on coding tasks paired with secure code (N = 6, 000).
rows.measure: Normalized harmfulness score; benchmark responses scored from 1 to 5 by GPT-4.1 and normalized to 0–1.
rows.note: Harmfulness decreased after secure-code retraining but remained above the base score of 0.08.
rows.check: Remove V7. Harm falls from 0.56 to 0.32, still well above the base of 0.08.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1 nano
rows.operation_detail: After insecure-code SFT, fine-tuned on coding tasks paired with secure code (N = 6, 000).
rows.measure: Normalized harmfulness score; benchmark responses scored from 1 to 5 by GPT-4.1 and normalized to 0–1.
rows.note: The paper says this increase was not significant; the realigned score is slightly higher than the misaligned score.
rows.check: Remove V7. Harm goes from 0.21 to 0.23 (p=0.31): no reversal, slightly higher after retraining.

relation.reason: Its own before-and-after harmfulness measurements test narrow-training transfer and benign retraining, alongside its main self-awareness question.

tranche.reason: The study measures behavioral transfer and subsequent realignment using a different harmfulness benchmark and sampling procedure from the original.

source_check.notes: Scores measure normalized harmfulness after maximum-of-ten selection, not single-response misalignment probabilities. Trivia induction and realignment results support the verdicts but are missing from the six listed rows.

statements.correction: Preprint, Section 3: 320 harm-provoking benchmark items; 10 responses per item; highest-harmfulness response retained; GPT-4.1 judge scores 1–5, normalized to 0–1. Table 11: full code harmfulness 0.41 before realignment, 0.17 afterward.
statements.problem: The preprint also selects the most harmful of ten responses; presenting this selection rule as a difference between sources is misleading.
